I. I NTRODUCTION
The problem of maximizing a non-negative monotone submodular function subject to a matroid constraint is one of earliest and most studied problems in submodular maximization.
The natural greedy algorithm obtains the optimal approximation ratio of 1− 1/e ≈ 0.632 for this problem when the matroid
constraint is restricted to be a cardinality constraint [1], [2].
However, the situation turned out to be much more involved
for general matroid constraints (or even partition matroid
constraints). In 1978, Fisher et al. showed that the natural
greedy algorithm guarantees a sub-optimal approximation ratio
of 1/2 for such constraints. This was improved (roughly 40
years later) by Călinescu et al. [3], who described a Continuous
Greedy algorithm obtaining the optimal approximation ratio
of 1 − 1/e for general matroid constraints. The Continuous
Greedy algorithm was a celebrated major improvement over
the state-of-the-art, but it has a significant drawback; namely,
it is based on a continuous extension of set functions termed
the multilinear extension. The only known way to evaluate the
multilinear extension is by sampling sets from an appropriate

Definition II.1. A set function f : 2N → R is submodular if
f (u | S) ≥ f (u | T ) for every two sets S ⊆ T ⊆ N and
element u ∈ N \ T .
An independence system is a pair (N , I), where N is a
ground set and I ⊆ 2N is a non-empty collection of subsets
of N that is down-closed in the sense that T ∈ I implies
that every set S ⊆ T also belongs to I. Following the
terminology used for linear spaces, it is customary to refer
to the sets of I as independent sets. Similarly, independent
sets that are inclusion-wise maximal (i.e., they are not subsets
of other independent sets) are called bases, and the size of the
largest base is called the rank of the independence system.
Throughout the paper, we use n to denote the size of the
ground set N and r to denote the rank of the independence
system.
A matroid is an independence system that also obeys the
following exchange axiom: if S, T are two independent sets
such that |S| < |T |, then there must exist an element u ∈ T \S
such that S ∪{u} ∈ I. Matroids have been extensively studied
as they capture many cases of interest, and at the same time,
enjoy a rich theoretical structure (see, e.g., [42]). However,
we mention here only two results about them. The first result,
which is an immediate corollary of exchange axiom, is that all
the bases of a matroid are of the same size (and thus, every
independent set of this size is a base). The other result is given
by the next lemma. In this lemma (and throughout the paper),
given a set S and element u, we use S + u and S − u as
shorthands for S ∪ {u} and S \ {u}, respectively.

Lemma II.3 (Lemma 3.2 in [7], based on [4]). Given a
non-negative monotone submodular function f and a matroid
M = (N , I), there exists a deterministic 1/3-approximation
algorithm for max{f (S) | S ∈ I} that has a query complexity
of O(n log r).

V. C ONCLUSION
In this work, we designed a deterministic non-oblivious
local search algorithm that has an approximation guarantee
of 1 − 1/e − ε for the problem of maximizing a monotone
submodular function subject to a matroid constraint. This
algorithm shows that there is essentially no separation between

submodular functions subject to a general matroid constraint.
Adding randomization, we showed that the query
√ complexity
of our algorithm can be improved to Oε (n + r n).
There are plenty of open questions that remain. The most
immediate of these is to find a way to further improve the running time of the randomized (or the deterministic) algorithm
to be nearly-linear
for all values of r (rather than just for
√
r = O( n) as in our work). A more subtle query complexity
question is related to the fact that, since a value oracle
query for the function g ′ defined in Section III-B requires
O(21/ε ) value oracle queries to f , the query complexities of
our algorithms depend exponentially on 1/ε. In other words,
our algorithms are efficient PTASs in the sense that their
query complexity is h(ε) · O(Poly(n, r)) for some function
h. A natural question is whether it is possible to design
a deterministic FPTAS for the problem we consider, i.e., a
deterministic algorithm obtaining (1 − 1/e − ε)-approximation
using O(Poly(n, r, ε−1 )) oracle queries. By guessing the most
valuable element of an optimal solution and setting ε to be
polynomially small, such an FPTAS will imply, in particular,
a deterministic algorithm guaranteeing a clean approximation
ratio of 1 − 1/e using O(Poly(n, r)) oracle queries.
A different direction is to use our new approach to design
deterministic (or randomized) algorithms for submodular objectives that are not guaranteed to be monotone. As discussed
above, following a long line of work, a recent paper of Buchbinder and Feldman [36] achieves the state-of-the-art 0.401approximation for this more general problem, while Oveis
Gharan and Vondrák [37] showed that no sub-exponential time
algorithm can obtain a better than 0.478-approximation. As the
algorithm of [36] is based on the multilinear extension, it is
inherently random. To the best of our knowledge, the currently
best deterministic algorithm for maximizing a non-negative
(not necessarily monotone) submodular function subject to a
matroid constraint guarantees only 1/4-approximation [47].
